items.prompt: How do a venomous snake's fangs get venom into its prey?

options.label: They channel it in like a hollow or grooved needle
options.feedback: A canal or groove runs down the fang, carrying venom from the gland straight into the wound as the fang sinks in.

options.label: They coat the wound with venom held on the tooth's surface
options.feedback: A surface coating would wash or wipe away before it could do much; the venom instead travels inside the fang itself.

options.label: The prey licks venom off the snake's mouth afterward
options.feedback: Nothing about a bite depends on the prey licking anything; the venom is delivered at the moment of the strike.

options.label: Venom seeps in through the prey's skin around the bite
options.feedback: Skin blocks venom fairly well; it has to be injected past that barrier through the fang, not spread on top of it.

items.ok_line: The fang works like a built-in needle.
items.ko_line: Look at the fang itself, not at what happens around it.
items.exp_title: A fang built like a needle
items.exp_text: A venomous snake's fang is hollow or deeply grooved along its length, connected at the base to a gland that stores venom under pressure from surrounding muscle. As the fang sinks into flesh, that pressure forces venom down the channel and out through an opening near the tip, straight into the wound rather than merely onto the skin's surface. The same design lets a snake control how much force it puts into squeezing the gland, changing how much venom actually enters the bite.

items.prompt: What is a "dry bite", and why does a snake sometimes deliver one?

options.label: A bite from a snake that has run out of venom permanently
options.feedback: A snake's venom glands refill over time; a dry bite is a choice made in the moment, not a permanent loss.

options.label: A bite aimed at dry ground rather than at flesh
options.feedback: The word describes how much venom is injected, not where or what the snake bites.

options.label: A bite in which the snake injects little or no venom on purpose
options.feedback: The muscles around the venom gland are under the snake's control, so it can hold venom back rather than spend it.

options.label: A bite where the venom has dried out and stopped working
options.feedback: Venom does not dry out inside a living snake; the gland keeps it in liquid form ready to use.

items.ok_line: Holding venom back is a choice the snake's own muscles make.
items.ko_line: The word is about how much venom goes in, not about the venom failing or running dry.
items.exp_text: The gland that stores a snake's venom is wrapped in muscle that the snake controls, the same way it controls any other muscle in its body. Producing venom costs the snake real energy, so when it strikes at a threat rather than at prey it means to eat, it often clenches that muscle only lightly or not at all, delivering little or no venom even though the fangs still puncture the skin. This is why a bite from a venomous snake does not always mean venom was actually injected.

items.prompt: How does venom help a snake overpower prey it could not simply outmuscle?

options.label: It coats the prey's skin so the snake can grip it more tightly
options.feedback: Venom is injected inside the prey, not smeared on the outside to improve the snake's grip.

options.label: It disables the prey's nerves or breaks down its tissue from within
options.feedback: Once inside, venom attacks nerve signals or living tissue directly, so struggling stops without the snake needing to overpower the prey by force.

options.label: It makes the prey too hot to keep moving
options.feedback: Venom does not work by raising temperature; its targets are nerves and tissue, not body heat.

options.label: It makes the prey's muscles grow suddenly tired from exercise
options.feedback: The prey is not being run to exhaustion; venom acts directly on nerve or tissue chemistry, often within moments of the bite.

items.ok_line: It fights the prey's body from the inside, not by brute strength.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the prey's own nerves and tissue once venom is inside.
items.exp_title: A fight fought from the inside
items.exp_text: Many prey animals are strong enough that a snake could never subdue them by muscle alone, so venom does the work of overpowering them from within instead. Once injected, it acts on the prey's own nerves or tissue, either scrambling the signals that let muscles move and cause paralysis, or breaking down living tissue so the body can no longer function normally. Either way, the prey is stopped, or dies, without the snake ever winning a contest of raw strength.

items.prompt: How does a snake manage to swallow prey much wider than its own head?

options.label: Its jawbones are loosely connected and its jaw ligaments stretch wide
options.feedback: The bones of a snake's jaw are not fused rigidly the way ours are, and the ligaments holding them stretch far enough to pass a bulky meal through.

options.label: It dislocates its skull and cannot close its mouth for days
options.feedback: The jaw stretches without actually dislocating, and a snake can close its mouth again as soon as the meal is down.

options.label: It breaks the meal into pieces with hidden back teeth
options.feedback: A snake's teeth grip and pull prey inward; they are not built to grind food into smaller pieces first.

options.label: It swallows only prey narrower than its head to begin with
options.feedback: Snakes regularly take prey noticeably wider than their own heads; the jaw's stretch is exactly what makes this possible.

items.ok_line: A loosely hinged, stretchable jaw does the work.
items.ko_line: Nothing is broken or dislocated here; the jaw is simply built to stretch.
items.exp_title: A jaw built to stretch, not to bite hard
items.exp_text: Unlike a mammal's jaw, a snake's lower jawbones are not fused together at the chin, and the bone connecting the jaw to the skull is only loosely hinged. Stretchy ligaments hold these pieces together instead of rigid joints, letting the whole structure spread far wider than the resting width of the head. The snake then walks each side of its jaw forward over the prey in turn, working it steadily inward until the stretched opening closes back around it.

items.prompt: How does a snake move forward across the ground without any legs?

options.label: By rolling its whole body sideways like a wheel
options.feedback: Ordinary snake movement is not a rolling motion; the body pushes against the ground rather than rotating over it.

options.label: By dragging itself using only its head muscles
options.feedback: The whole body contributes to movement, not just muscles near the head pulling the rest along.

options.label: By hopping in short bursts using its tail as a spring
options.feedback: A snake has no legs or springy tail built for hopping; its motion is a continuous push against the ground.

options.label: By pushing curves of its body sideways against uneven ground
options.feedback: Muscles running the length of the body throw it into a series of curves, and each curve shoves sideways against a bump or edge in the ground to drive the snake forward.

items.ok_line: Every curve of the body becomes a point to push against.
items.ko_line: There is no rolling or hopping here; look at what each curve of the body does against the ground.
items.exp_title: Curves that push against the ground
items.exp_text: A snake's body is thrown into a series of S-shaped curves by muscles running along its length, and each curve presses sideways against whatever irregularity the ground offers, a stone, a root, or simply looser soil. As one curve pushes back against that point, it drives the snake's body forward past it, and the next curve behind takes over the same job in turn. The motion works because the snake's body has far more points of contact with the ground than a walking animal's legs would give it.

items.prompt: How can some snakes sense the body heat of warm prey even in complete darkness?

options.label: By tasting the warmth of the air with the tongue
options.feedback: The tongue collects scent particles for smell, not heat; sensing warmth itself is a separate sense using a different organ.

options.label: By hearing the faint sound the prey's body heat makes
options.feedback: Heat produces no sound of its own; what these snakes detect is infrared radiation, not a noise.

options.label: Through pit organs on the face that detect infrared radiation
options.feedback: These pits contain a thin membrane sensitive enough to register the faint infrared heat glowing off a warm body, even without any light at all.

options.label: By feeling ground vibrations made by the prey's warm muscles
options.feedback: Vibration sensing exists too, but it responds to movement through the ground, not to heat given off by a body.

items.ok_line: A dedicated organ reads heat the way an eye reads light.
items.ko_line: This sense is neither taste, hearing, nor touch; it is a separate way of detecting warmth itself.
items.exp_title: An organ built to read heat
items.exp_text: Pit vipers and some other snakes carry a pair of small pits on the face, each lined with a thin membrane packed with heat-sensitive nerve endings. Infrared radiation, the invisible heat given off by any warm body, strikes this membrane and triggers those nerves, building a rough picture of where warmth is coming from. The brain can combine the signal from both pits into something like a heat picture layered over the snake's ordinary sight, letting it strike accurately at prey it cannot see at all.

items.prompt: Why does a snake flick its forked tongue in and out of its mouth?

options.label: To cool the inside of its mouth in warm weather
options.feedback: Cooling is not the tongue's job here; the flicking continues in cool weather just as much as in warm.

options.label: To gather scent particles from the air and pass them to a smell organ
options.feedback: The two tips of the tongue pick up scent particles from different points in the air, then touch them against an organ in the roof of the mouth that reads them as smell.

options.label: To test whether nearby surfaces are safe to touch
options.feedback: The tongue is not a touch sensor for surfaces; its job is collecting airborne scent, not testing texture or safety.

options.label: To signal aggression to a rival snake
options.feedback: Tongue-flicking is a constant habit used for smelling the surroundings, not a threat display aimed at rivals.

items.ok_line: The tongue is a scent-collector, not a mouth or a weapon.
items.ko_line: Think about what the two tips of the forked tongue are gathering from the air.
items.exp_title: A tongue built to carry scent inward
items.exp_text: Each flick of a snake's tongue sweeps its two forked tips through the air or across the ground, picking up tiny scent particles on their moist surface. Drawn back into the mouth, the tips are pressed against an organ in the roof of the mouth that reads chemical signals the way a nose reads smells. Because the two tips sample slightly different points in space, the snake can even tell which side a scent is stronger on, helping it track a trail in a chosen direction.

items.prompt: How does a rattlesnake's rattle produce its buzzing sound?

options.label: Loosely linked hollow segments clatter against each other when shaken
options.feedback: Each segment is a hollow shell that stays loosely hooked to the next, so shaking the tail makes them knock together rapidly.

options.label: Air is forced through a narrow whistle-like opening in the tail
options.feedback: No air passage is involved; the sound comes from solid segments striking one another, not from air moving through anything.

options.label: The snake grinds its teeth together at the tip of its tail
options.feedback: Teeth play no part in this; the tail carries hardened segments made from the same material as the snake's scales.

options.label: Scales along the tail vibrate against the ground
options.feedback: The rattle works even when the tail is held above the ground; the segments strike each other, not the surface below.

items.ok_line: Hollow segments knocking together make the sound.
items.ko_line: No air, teeth, or ground contact is involved; think about the segments themselves.
items.exp_text: A rattlesnake's rattle is built from a chain of hollow, interlocking segments made of the same tough material as the snake's scales, loosely hooked to one another rather than fused solid. When muscles at the base of the tail shake the whole chain rapidly, each segment knocks against its neighbors, and the dry clatter of these collisions is what produces the buzzing sound. A new segment is added each time the snake sheds its skin, so the rattle keeps rebuilding itself throughout its owner's life.

items.prompt: Why does venom help a snake begin digesting its prey before the meal is even swallowed?

options.label: It coats the outside of the prey to soften the skin for easier grip
options.feedback: The softening happens inside the prey's own tissue, not on the outer surface where the snake's grip is concerned.

options.label: It cools the prey's body so it decays faster before swallowing
options.feedback: Venom does not work by temperature or decay; the breakdown it causes is chemical, and it starts almost immediately, well before decay would ever begin.

options.label: It replaces the need for the snake's own stomach acid entirely
options.feedback: The stomach still finishes the job; venom only gets a head start on breaking tissue down before digestion in the stomach even begins.

options.label: Its enzymes start breaking down tissue from the inside as soon as it is injected
options.feedback: Many venoms contain enzymes closely related to digestive ones, and once injected they begin dismantling proteins inside the prey right away, ahead of the stomach's own work.

items.ok_line: Digestion effectively begins the moment the bite lands.
items.ko_line: The breakdown happens chemically, inside the prey, and it starts well before swallowing.
items.exp_text: Snake venom evolved from ordinary saliva, and in many species it still carries enzymes closely related to the ones used for digestion, only far more concentrated and now delivered by injection. Once inside the prey, these enzymes begin breaking down proteins and other tissue from within, well before the prey has even been swallowed. By the time the snake's own stomach gets to work, a meal that arrived through venom has already had a considerable head start toward being broken down.

items.prompt: Why doesn't a venomous snake generally harm itself if it accidentally swallows some of its own venom?

options.label: Its own venom glands make a separate, harmless version for the snake itself
options.feedback: A snake carries only one kind of venom in its glands; there is no separate harmless version made for its own use.

options.label: Venom loses its effect the moment it leaves the fang
options.feedback: Venom stays fully active once delivered; that is exactly why a bite works. The safety here comes from a different route entirely.

options.label: Digestive acid in the stomach breaks the venom's proteins apart before they can act
options.feedback: Venom is built almost entirely of proteins, and like any protein eaten as food, it gets dismantled by stomach acid and digestive enzymes rather than being absorbed intact.

options.label: The snake's blood contains a built-in antidote to its own venom
options.feedback: No built-in antidote circulates in the blood for this purpose; the protection instead comes from how the digestive tract handles proteins that are swallowed rather than injected.

items.ok_line: Swallowed venom meets the same fate as any other protein in a meal.
items.ko_line: Nothing here relies on an antidote or a special harmless venom; think about what the stomach does to any protein.
items.exp_title: Venom needs a wound, not a stomach
items.exp_text: Venom is dangerous only when it reaches the bloodstream or tissue directly through a wound, where its proteins can act on nerves or cells before anything interferes with them. Swallowed rather than injected, venom instead enters the stomach, where acid and digestive enzymes break its proteins apart the same way they would break down any other protein in a meal. Taken apart into harmless fragments before it can be absorbed, the venom never gets the chance to act the way it would from a bite.
